overview: Monday's news is dominated by a sharp India-Italy political spat, a confirmed Xi-Trump-Putin summit, and a widening Iran-linked conflict that is still hitting Gulf air travel, alongside a weaker China economy and a steadier Indian market.

items.headline: Italian socialist's 'vote chor' remark at Bharat Summit sparks BJP-Congress row
items.summary: Giacomo Filibeck, Secretary General of the Party of European Socialists, made a 'vote chor' (vote thief) remark on the sidelines of the Congress-organised Bharat Summit 2026 in Hyderabad, and the BJP has objected strongly.
items.detail: The BJP lodged a complaint with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office in Hyderabad, calling the remarks provocative and seeking action against the foreign delegate, including visa cancellation and deportation. Telangana BJP chief N Ramchander Rao called the event an 'anti-Bharat Summit'. A Meloni ally, meanwhile, told the Italian socialist it was inappropriate to lecture India on democracy. Congress has been using the 'vote chori' theme around electoral rolls, which the BJP says is being used to attack India abroad.
items.analysis: The row sits on top of a wider debate about voter-roll revisions in India, and it shows how foreign party leaders can become part of domestic political fights. Watch whether the FRRO complaint leads to any formal step.

items.headline: China confirms first Xi-Trump-Putin summit for 19 November
items.summary: China has confirmed a summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on 19 November, which would be the first meeting of the three leaders together.
items.detail: Reports describe the meeting as a China-Russia-US summit to be held in Shenzhen, and Financial Times coverage frames it as part of a busy week of high-stakes Asian diplomacy. The agenda is still being discussed by the outlets reporting on it. Trade and chip export controls are already in the background, with Nvidia-related disputes expected to feature in the wider US-China relationship. Japan has expressed concern that the three powers could draw closer together at its expense.
items.analysis: A three-way meeting of this kind would be unusual and could reshape expectations about US-China and US-Russia relations. Its concrete outcomes remain unknown until after 19 November.

items.headline: Iran threatens two US Navy officers as a third US carrier reaches the Middle East
items.summary: Iran's embassy has threatened two US Navy officers it says ordered the Minab school strike, while the US has moved a third aircraft carrier into the Middle East as the conflict continues.
items.detail: The threat, reported as 'we will find you', was issued as a US warship returned home from the region. Live coverage reports that a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East. Iran has also been in the news for attacks around the region, with Bahrain saying it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks after a nationwide alert. The broader war has been affecting flights and hotels across the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
items.analysis: A rising military presence combined with direct threats against named officers raises the risk of further escalation. Gulf aviation and tourism are feeling the effects already.

items.headline: Iran rules out UN inspections of damaged nuclear sites until the war ends
items.summary: Iran has said UN inspectors will not be allowed into its damaged nuclear sites until the war is over.
items.detail: The position was reported by The New Indian Express on Monday. It leaves the International Atomic Energy Agency without access to sites that were hit during the conflict. Iran's foreign minister Araqchi has blamed what he calls US-Israeli aggression for the insecurity in the Gulf. Western governments have typically pressed for inspections to verify the state of Iran's nuclear programme.
items.analysis: Without inspections, outside observers have limited independent information about the damage and the status of Iran's nuclear material. Watch for any change in position once fighting stops.

items.headline: China's economy slows more than expected in October
items.summary: Industrial output, retail sales and investment in China all came in below forecasts in October, despite a government stimulus push.
items.detail: Bloomberg, Reuters, CNBC and the Financial Times all reported the miss on Monday. Demand for Chinese goods abroad has been strong, according to the Wall Street Journal, but momentum at home is slowing. Some analysts also point to succession and stability questions in China as a longer-term concern. The data adds to pressure on Beijing to do more to support growth.
items.analysis: A slower China matters for Asian exporters, commodity prices and global demand. The gap between strong exports and weak domestic activity is the key contrast to watch.

items.headline: ASEAN and China fall short of agreeing a South China Sea code
items.summary: ASEAN and China did not reach agreement on a code of conduct for the South China Sea at the latest round of talks.
items.detail: The code has been under negotiation for years, with the aim of reducing the risk of incidents among rival claimants in the disputed waters. The meeting took place alongside the ASEAN summit in Manila, where Philippine President called for greater regional unity amid geopolitical tensions. Prime Minister Modi is also in the Philippines, where he highlighted ASEAN's role in India's Act East policy.
items.analysis: The failure to agree a code keeps a long-running dispute unresolved. Its practical effect depends on how the parties handle incidents at sea in the months ahead.

items.headline: US air travel recovers slowly after a nationwide ground stop
items.summary: A nationwide ground stop of US flights has raised questions about the country's aviation infrastructure, and thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed.
items.detail: Reports say the disruption was linked to a faulty router, and the FAA is investigating. The FAA chief has said US air travel should be back to normal by Sunday, while the BBC reported thousands of flights cancelled or delayed in the days after the grounding. Commentators have pointed to the air traffic control system and to a single router in southern Arkansas as points of weakness.
items.analysis: The episode shows how dependent modern air travel is on a small number of technical systems. Investigations and any changes to the air traffic control setup will be closely watched.

items.headline: Quad leaders to meet in Manila as the US denies the grouping is faltering
items.summary: Ahead of a Quad meeting in Manila, the US has pushed back on reports that the grouping of India, Japan, Australia and the US is losing momentum under Trump.
items.detail: Japan Today reports that Trump and other Quad leaders are due to meet in Manila on Tuesday, though one outlet describes the leaders' meeting as possible rather than confirmed. Commentary from ORF Online describes the challenge of holding the grouping together. The Quad brings together four democracies that share concerns about China's influence in the Indo-Pacific.
items.analysis: The meeting will test whether the Quad can keep its agenda on track despite differences in approach among members. Watch for statements on maritime security and supply chains.

items.headline: Election Commission tells the Supreme Court voters deleted in the roll revision can re-enrol without prosecution
items.summary: The Election Commission has assured the Supreme Court that voters wrongly excluded during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) can apply again using Form 6 without fear of prosecution.
items.detail: In new affidavits, the Commission said measures are in place to re-enrol voters who were wrongly excluded from the draft roll. Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress has also submitted affidavits to the Commission in compliance with a Supreme Court order. Opposition parties have questioned the verification drive, and some commentary asks why the exercise has put the poll body under scrutiny. The Commission Chief Gyanesh Kumar has said pure electoral rolls are the bedrock of democracy.
items.analysis: The row is about the balance between cleaning up rolls and making sure eligible voters are not left out. The Supreme Court's view on the affidavits will shape the next steps.

items.headline: Bengal police encounters and a Chhath remark draw political fire
items.summary: A man accused of firing at a policeman in Santiniketan was killed in a police encounter, the fifth such death in West Bengal in six months, while a TMC MP's remark on Chhath has triggered a row.
items.detail: Reports say Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari warned criminals that there is 'no place for goons' after the encounter, and critics have described it as a fifth 'encounter' killing under the BJP government. Separately, Trinamool MP Kalyan Banerjee's remarks on Bihari migrants and Chhath Puja prompted BJP criticism and a swipe from Adhikari at Raj Thackeray. The Chief Minister has said the earlier government considered only Muslims as a minority.
items.analysis: Questions about police encounters and about how political leaders talk about migrants are likely to continue. Both sides are using the episodes in their broader campaigns.

items.headline: Parliament's winter session likely in early December, with the delimitation bill in focus
items.summary: The winter session of Parliament is expected in the first week of December, with the delimitation bill and the women's quota bill expected to be key items.
items.detail: Reports from India Today, Rediff and the Times of India say the session is likely to start in December. Deccan Herald notes uncertainty over the delimitation bill. The women's reservation bill is described as facing a key test. Parliament's recent tributes to Birsa Munda also drew a row, with the BJP criticising the Congress for being absent.
items.analysis: The session's agenda will show how far the government can push its priorities on seat allocation and women's representation. Opposition support is central to both.

items.headline: High Court directs Kerala government to set up family courts within four weeks
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has directed the state government to expedite the establishment of family courts, preferably within four weeks.
items.detail: The direction comes as part of the court's concern about delays in family disputes. The state government is responsible for setting up the courts and providing staff and infrastructure. Weekly round-ups from LiveLaw show the court has been active on several other issues in the same week, including questioning police curbs on DJ parties and floating a proposal to lower the juvenile age.
items.analysis: Whether the four-week timeline is met will be a useful test of how quickly the state can act on court directions in family law.

items.headline: Keralam government defends VEH power deal, as regulator seeks clarifications
items.summary: The Keralam government says a power deal with VEH Global is meant to address a critical power deficit, while the state electricity regulator KSERC has sought clarifications.
items.detail: The Hindu reports that the government has presented the agreement as a response to a shortfall in supply. The regulator is examining the terms and has asked for further information before it is satisfied. Power purchase agreements in Kerala are usually reviewed by the regulator to check pricing and supply commitments, so the clarifications are a normal part of that process.
items.analysis: The regulator's response will show whether the deal meets the state's supply needs at a reasonable cost. Peak-season demand will keep the issue in the news.

items.headline: Thrissur Pooram probe: government sends back Crime Branch report
items.summary: The Keralam government has flagged major omissions in the Crime Branch's probe into the disruption of the Thrissur Pooram festival and sent the report back.
items.detail: Onmanorama reports the Home Department has rejected the SIT report, creating a further hurdle for the investigation. The disruption of the temple festival has been a politically sensitive matter in the state. The government's objections are about gaps in the report rather than about the outcome of the case.
items.analysis: The probe's direction now depends on whether the investigators can fill the gaps the government has identified. The case has public interest because of the festival's importance in Thrissur.

items.headline: MP seeks fair compensation and rehabilitation for families affected by the Great Nicobar project
items.summary: Andaman and Nicobar MP Bishnu Pada Ray has pressed for strict compliance with land acquisition law and a fair compensation package for families affected by the Great Nicobar project.
items.detail: Ray raised the demand in the Lok Sabha and ahead of a rehabilitation and resettlement committee meeting for the Great Nicobar International Airport project. The Great Nicobar project has been controversial because of its potential effects on forests, the environment and tribal communities. Ray's remarks focus on the procedural and financial side of displacement rather than the project's overall approval.
items.analysis: Rehabilitation terms and land acquisition compliance are where local concerns about the project are most often tested. The committee's decisions will be a useful indicator.

items.headline: Sri Lankan firm wins $75 million contract for a power plant in the Andamans
items.summary: Sri Lanka's Lakdhanavi has won a contract worth about $75 million to build a 57 MW power plant in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
items.detail: Reports from Rediff, BusinessLine and the Daily Excelsior all describe the same contract. A 57 MW plant would be a significant addition to the islands' power supply, which relies heavily on imported diesel. Island power projects are often built to reduce costs and improve reliability for remote communities.
items.analysis: The project's timeline and the supply arrangements for diesel and transmission will determine how much it changes the islands' energy picture.

items.headline: Bay of Bengal depression set to become Cyclone Akvan, with Andhra Pradesh on alert
items.summary: A depression over the Bay of Bengal is expected to strengthen into Cyclone Akvan, and coastal Andhra Pradesh has been put on alert.
items.detail: Down To Earth's daily weather tracker reports the system is on track to become a cyclone. Earlier warnings had already affected ferry services to the Andamans, and the islands are regularly exposed to storms from this basin. Cyclone warnings typically lead to suspended ferry trips and precautionary evacuations in vulnerable areas.
items.analysis: The track and strength of the storm will decide whether the impact is limited to the coast or reaches the islands. Forecasts are the thing to watch.

items.headline: UAE Central Bank says insurers must cover organ donation and transplant costs
items.summary: The UAE Central Bank has said insurers must cover the costs of organ donation and transplantation, including for donors and recipients.
items.detail: Gulf News, Gulf Today and Khaleej Times all reported the requirement on Sunday, describing it as covering transplant-related care for life in some cases. The rule extends the scope of health cover for a set of procedures that are expensive and often long-term. The rule applies to insurers operating in the UAE and is likely to affect how policies are priced and written.
items.analysis: For residents and insurers, the practical question is how the rule is applied to existing policies and how the costs are split over time. Details will come from the regulator.

items.headline: IRDAI likely to revise insurance distribution norms after industry pushback
items.summary: India's insurance regulator IRDAI is reported to be considering changes to its distribution rules after industry feedback.
items.detail: Moneycontrol and NewsBytes report that the regulator has received around 200 comments on the proposed overhaul and may tweak the norms. Distribution rules govern how agents, brokers and bancassurance partners sell policies, so changes affect commissions and sales models. Industry groups have argued that some of the draft rules could be impractical.
items.analysis: Whether the final rules are softened will show how the regulator balances consumer protection with the commercial needs of distributors and insurers.

items.headline: CCI approves Go Digit merger with Infoworks Services
items.summary: India's Competition Commission (CCI) has approved the merger of Go Digit General Insurance with Infoworks Services.
items.detail: The approval was reported by scanx.trade on Sunday. Competition clearance is a standard step before a merger can proceed, and it checks whether the deal would reduce competition in a market. The report does not give the deal's financial terms.
items.analysis: Competition approval is an important hurdle, but the next steps and the deal's effect on Go Digit's business will depend on details not yet in the reports.

items.headline: Dubai airport resumes flights after an Iran drone strike
items.summary: Dubai airport has resumed flights after an Iranian drone strike, while a missile strike in Abu Dhabi killed one person.
items.detail: DD News reported the airport's resumption on Monday. Gulf News' daily update for residents also covers the conflict's effects. Travel links through the Gulf have been disrupted during the war, and airlines have revised schedules and cancelled some routes. Travellers should check with their airlines for current status.
items.analysis: Airport operations have been stop-start during the conflict, so flight status is changing quickly. The situation depends on how the wider war develops.

items.headline: UAE hotels still struggling as the Iran conflict drags on
items.summary: Travel Weekly reports there is no relief yet for hotels in the UAE and Saudi Arabia while the Iran conflict continues.
items.detail: Hotels in the region depend heavily on international visitors, and the conflict has reduced demand. DW has described Dubai as feeling like a ghost city during the war. Hotel occupancy and rates are closely linked to flight availability and to travel advisories from governments abroad.
items.analysis: The hotel sector's recovery depends on the war's end and on confidence among travellers, neither of which is clear yet.

items.headline: One in five UAE adults has diabetes, with cases could reach 1.9 million by 2050
items.summary: A new estimate says about one in five UAE adults has diabetes, and the number of cases could reach 1.9 million by 2050.
items.detail: Emirates 24|7 reports the projection on Sunday. Diabetes is one of the country's main chronic health concerns, and its management affects health-care costs and insurance premiums. Long-term projections like this one are often used to plan prevention programmes and health coverage.
items.analysis: The projection suggests that prevention and early screening will be a continuing priority for public health and for private insurers.

items.headline: Sensex and Nifty rally as foreign investors return and crude eases
items.summary: Indian indices rose in early trade on Monday, helped by strong foreign fund inflows and lower crude oil prices.
items.detail: Moneycontrol reports the Sensex gained about 600 points and Nifty moved above 25,300 at one point, while other outlets gave smaller gains. Foreign investors have reportedly put about $8.9 billion into Indian equities in November. India Today notes the Sensex has gained more than 10,600 points over roughly 26 sessions, although valuations and global risks remain. Gains were not uniform, and the market pared some of its gains later in the session.
items.analysis: Foreign flows and oil prices are the two main drivers. A sustained rally would depend on whether those flows hold, and on how the Iran conflict and US rate expectations develop.

items.headline: Rupee firms to 94.13 against the dollar on foreign inflows and easing oil
items.summary: The rupee rose 6 paise to 94.13 against the US dollar in early trade on Monday.
items.detail: Reuters said the currency was supported by foreign inflows and corporate dollar sales. Lower crude prices also eased pressure on the rupee, since India imports much of its oil. Finshots asks whether the RBI has really stabilised the currency, and FXStreet notes that expectations of a firm Fed are a counterweight.
items.analysis: The rupee's direction is closely tied to oil and to the strength of the dollar, so both will matter for the currency in the coming days.

items.headline: Brent falls to $96 as supply outlook improves, while gold hits a one-year low
items.summary: Brent crude has fallen to $96 a barrel on an improved supply outlook, and gold has dropped to its lowest level in over a year.
items.detail: APAC Media reports Brent's fall as supply prospects improve despite the Middle East conflict. Reuters reports gold hit its lowest level in more than a year, weighed down by a firm dollar and the Fed outlook. Traders' expectations of a December rate rise, reported by Traders Union, also weigh on gold, which does not pay interest.
items.analysis: Oil and gold are moving on different pressures: supply for oil, and interest rate expectations for gold. Both are sensitive to developments in the Gulf and the Fed's next steps.

items.headline: India's Semicon 2.0 scheme approved with Rs 1.27 lakh crore
items.summary: The Cabinet has approved a Rs 1.27 lakh crore second phase of India's semiconductor programme, called Semicon 2.0.
items.detail: DD News reports the approval on Monday. The government's broader push includes chip fabrication and assembly, and IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has said India needs to scale up semiconductors to be a serious global player. Noel Tata has also spoken about semiconductors and EV batteries as partnerships in India's development.
items.analysis: The scheme's effect will depend on the projects that get funded and on whether they reach production. Watch for the first approvals under it.

items.headline: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi raises $24 million seed round
items.summary: Bengaluru-based chip startup Bharat Semi has raised a $24 million seed round to develop AI sensor chips for global markets.
items.detail: TechCrunch and India Today both report the round, with India Today putting the amount at about Rs 215 crore. The company says it is aiming at the global AI sensor market. Large seed rounds for chip companies are unusual, reflecting investor interest in semiconductor design from India.
items.analysis: A large seed round signals strong investor appetite for Indian chip design, though the company still has to show products and customers.

items.headline: US plans to name Nvidia and other AI firms as national champions
items.summary: The Trump administration is reportedly planning to name Nvidia and other AI firms as US 'national champions', according to the Wall Street Journal.
items.detail: Reuters reports the plan, and the Times of India says it includes Microsoft and Amazon among 20-plus companies. The report says China is the 'target' of the designation. The news comes amid a row over Nvidia that was also linked to a supply-chain accord India and the US signed on AI supply chains from China.
items.analysis: A government label of this kind could bring support or scrutiny to chosen firms. The details of what the designation actually means are not yet clear.

items.headline: Samsung and Xiaomi raise phone prices in India after Diwali
items.summary: Samsung and Xiaomi have raised smartphone prices in India by up to 19 per cent, a few weeks after Diwali sales.
items.detail: Moneycontrol reports the increases, and other outlets say budget and mid-range Samsung and Redmi models have also become costlier. Companies often adjust prices after promotional periods, and component costs in the memory chip market have been rising. The increases follow a period of heavy discounting.
items.analysis: Higher phone prices are a sign of how memory and component costs are passing through to consumers, and of how promotions can mask underlying price pressures.

items.headline: New nickel catalyst could make hydrogen from ammonia cheaper without ruthenium
items.summary: Researchers have reported a nickel-based catalyst that releases hydrogen from ammonia without using ruthenium, a costly precious metal.
items.detail: BigGo Finance reports that the catalyst aims to reduce supply costs for hydrogen production from ammonia. Ammonia is attractive as a hydrogen carrier because it is easier to store and transport than hydrogen gas. Ruthenium catalysts have been the standard in this approach, so a cheaper alternative based on nickel could matter for the economics of hydrogen as an energy carrier.
items.analysis: Whether the catalyst performs at industrial scale will decide its usefulness. Cost reductions only matter if efficiency and durability hold up.

items.headline: AI and experiments reveal impurities that hinder recycling of waste plastic pyrolysis oil
items.summary: A study combining AI with lab experiments has identified impurities that get in the way of recycling oil made from waste plastic by pyrolysis.
items.detail: Newswise reports that the researchers used machine learning alongside experiments to find which contaminants interfere with the process. Pyrolysis heats waste plastic without oxygen to produce an oil that can, in principle, be refined into fuels or new plastics. Impurities are a common reason these oils are hard to upgrade, so identifying them is a useful step.
items.analysis: Knowing which impurities cause problems points to where cleaning or pre-treatment steps should focus. The approach may be useful for other waste-to-fuel processes.

items.headline: arXiv paper: electric fields may make grain boundaries in Li2O easier paths for lithium ions
items.summary: A new arXiv preprint simulates how electric fields affect lithium-ion movement in Li2O, a battery-related material, and finds that boundaries between crystal grains can become fast routes.
items.detail: In plain terms, the authors ask whether ions move in a battery the same way they do when a material is at rest. Using electric-field molecular dynamics, they compare bulk Li2O with its grain boundaries, which are the interfaces between tiny crystal regions. Their finding is that boundaries that normally trap vacancies can become pathways for lithium ions when a field is applied.
items.analysis: This is a simulation study, so it has not been tested in a real battery. It is useful for understanding how ions behave under the operating conditions batteries actually face.

items.headline: arXiv paper: machine learning predicts electron density for device simulations
items.summary: A new arXiv preprint presents DeltaChargeNet, a machine-learning model that predicts electron density from atomic structure to speed up electronic and quantum transport simulations.
items.detail: In plain English, electron density describes where electrons sit around atoms, and calculating it accurately is slow with standard quantum methods. The model is combined with a tight-binding electronic structure method so that devices and materials can be simulated more quickly. The paper's aim is to make device-level transport calculations more practical.
items.analysis: Machine-learning shortcuts like this are a growing part of computational materials research. Their value depends on accuracy across a wide range of materials.

items.headline: Scientists count 788 species on a Pacific seabed patch targeted for mining
items.summary: A study of a patch of Pacific seafloor targeted for mining found 788 species, most new to science, and showed fewer animals where a mining machine had passed.
items.detail: Futura reports that the researchers counted animals in the area and found that where a mining machine had passed, animal numbers dropped by 37 per cent. The finding adds data to the debate about deep-sea mining, a topic that gets much less attention than land-based mining. Because many species in the patch were new to science, the study also underlines how little is known about these habitats.
items.analysis: The results are likely to feed into discussions about whether deep-sea mining can be done without serious ecological damage. Further data would strengthen the picture.

items.headline: David Ebert's decades of searching for lost shark species
items.summary: Mongabay profiles marine researcher David Ebert and his life spent searching for 'lost sharks', species that have been hard to find or describe.
items.detail: The profile covers how Ebert has worked with fish markets to find specimens that scientists have not documented in the wild. Many shark species are known only from a few records, and fish markets have sometimes turned up animals that field surveys missed. The story is a reminder that taxonomy and conservation still depend heavily on field detective work.
items.analysis: Finding these species is important for setting conservation priorities, since a species cannot be protected if scientists do not know it exists.
